metadata.title: Garner v. Jones, 529 U.S. 244 (2000) (No. 99-137)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Garner v. Jones

Opinion filed: 2000-04-18

Docket No.: 99-137

Citations:
• 146 L. Ed. 2d 236
• 120 S. Ct. 1362
• 529 U.S. 244
• 2000 U.S. LEXIS 2346

Case holding summaries:
• declining to “micromanage[]” ever-evolving parole procedures
• requiring a prisoner to show that “as applied to his own sentence the law created a significant risk of increasing his punishment”
• stating inquiry is whether new rule “creates a significant risk of prolonging respondent’s incarceration”
• announcing the rule that, to prove an ex post facto violation related to changes in parole procedures, an inmate must, “show that as applied to his own sentence the law created a significant risk of increasing his punishment”
• “Retroactive changes in laws governing parole of prisoners, in some instances, may be violative of [the ex post facto clause].”
• applying the parole regime in effect when the inmate committed his second offense: escape from prison
• stating inquiry is whether new rule "creates a significant risk of prolonging respondent's incarceration"
• addressing the Georgia rule at issue in the instant case
• emphasizing the need for evidence respecting the practical implementation of the parole rule and remanding to allow the respondent an opportunity to develop such proof
• recognizing that a change in a parole board’s rules could, given an adequate showing, run afoul of the Ex Post Facto Clause
• remanding to Eleventh Circuit because the court of appeals failed to consider the specific effects of the parole reconsideration statute
• considering the parole board's discretion to determine how often to set parole reconsideration dates
• considering the parole board's discretion to expedite parole reviews to consider new information
• quot- ing California Dept. of Corrections v. Morales, 514 U. S. 499, 509 (1995)
• upholding Georgia administrative regulation changing frequency of parole hearings for prisoners serving life sentences from every three years to every eight years against ex post facto challenge
• considering whether an amendment to a Georgia rule that changed parole reconsideration review procedures violated the Ex Post Facto Clause
• “Retroactive changes in laws governing parole of prisoners, in some instances, may be violative of this precept [against retroactively increasing punishment].”
• applying ex post facto analysis to changes in executive branch policy
• no ex post facto clause violation because defendant did not prove that the amendment created a significant risk of increased punishment
• court presumed, in a case involving an internal rule that affected the rights of prisoners, that an agency follows its internal policies
• noting that vesting the Board with discretion to impose a longer set-off between parole reviews merely gives the Board “a more careful and accurate exercise of [its] discretion”
• “Absent a demonstration to the contrary, we presume the Board follows its statutory commands and internal policies in fulfilling its obligations.”
• "In the case before us, respondent must show that as applied to his own sentence the law created a significant risk of increasing his punishment."
• explaining that a legal change violates the Ex Post Facto Clause when it creates “a significant risk of increasing [the defendant’s] punishment”
• "Absent a demonstration to the contrary, we presume the [b]oard follows its statutory commands and internal policies in fulfilling its obligations"
• remanding case for further consideration whether retroactive application of amendment created "significant risk of increased punishment for [the individual]," because record revealed only "speculation"
• "requisite risk" can either be "inherent in the framework of amended [statute or] demonstrated on the record"
• "One function of the Ex Post Facto Clause is to bar enactments which, by retroactive operation, increase the punishment for a crime after its commission."
• remanding to consider discovery because “[t]he record before the Court of Appeals contained little information bearing on the level of risk created by the change in law.”
• “The case turns on the [retroactive] operation of the amendment to Rule 475-3-.05-2.”
• announcing the rule that, to prove an ex post facto violation related to changes in parole procedures, an inmate must, "show that as applied to his own sentence the law created a significant risk of increasing his punishment"
• The ex post facto doctrine carries “some idea of actual or constructive notice to the criminal before commission of the offense of the penalty for the transgression . . . .”
• “In the [Ex Post Facto Clause] case before us, respondent must show that as applied to his own sentence[,] the [change in] law created a significant risk of increasing his punishment.”
• decreasing frequency of rehearings not a per se ex post facto violation
• “Whether retroactive application of a particular change in parole law respects the prohibition on ex post facto legislation is often a question of particular difficulty when the discretion vested in a parole board is taken into account.”
